expansion:
Choroiditis is the keyed diagnosis because the lecture defines posterior uveitis in exactly these terms on its classification slide: “SLIDE 12 — Uveitis: anatomical classification... 3. Posterior uveitis: (Choroiditis – Chorioretinitis) — Inflammation of the choroid with or without inflammation of the retina” (L13,14, slide 12). Multifocal yellowish-grey patches with well-demarcated borders are the appearance of active choroidal inflammatory foci, and areas of chorioretinal atrophy with pigmented borders alongside them are the scarred, healed lesions left by earlier episodes of the same inflammatory process — a mixture of active and healed lesions is the classic picture of a recurrent or multifocal choroiditis.

Exudative retinal detachment, option B, is a separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium caused by fluid accumulating beneath it, typically from a choroidal or vascular process; it does not itself present as multifocal yellowish-grey chorioretinal patches with pigmented, well-demarcated atrophic borders — those atrophic, demarcated scars are a feature of resolved focal inflammation, not of a detachment, which instead produces a bullous, mobile retinal elevation (not taken from the course material).

Retinitis pigmentosa, option C, is a progressive, usually bilateral hereditary photoreceptor dystrophy classically presenting with bone-spicule pigmentation, attenuated vessels and waxy disc pallor, a pattern that is diffuse and symmetric rather than multifocal patches with discrete atrophic borders; it does not match the described pattern of discrete yellowish-grey lesions plus separate pigmented-border atrophic patches (not taken from the course material).

Retinal vasculitis, option D, is inflammation centred on the retinal vessels themselves, producing perivascular sheathing, haemorrhages and vascular leakage rather than the described well-demarcated yellowish-grey choroidal patches and pigmented atrophic scars; the fundus picture in the stem centres on choroidal/chorioretinal lesions, not on vessel sheathing, so it points away from a primarily vascular process (not taken from the course material).
objective: Recognise multifocal chorioretinal lesions with pigmented atrophic scarring as choroiditis (posterior uveitis)
